findings.description: subprocess.run(["rustc", "--version"]) in setup.py error handler — no shell, fixed argument list, no external input; not command injection
findings.reasoning: The flagged subprocess call is a hardcoded argument vector (["rustc", "--version"]) with no shell=True and no interpolation of any external, environment- or user-controlled data. It is only reached inside an exception handler in setup.py that prints debug assistance when a build fails. There is no attacker-controlled input reaching this call, so the py/shell-invocation-sweep hit on "process spawning" is not an exploitable injection vector. Additionally this is packaging/build-time code (setup.py), not library runtime code.

findings.description: hashlib.sha1 used only to derive an X.509 key identifier (RFC 5280 method 1) — standardized identifier derivation, not a security-relevant collision-resistance primitive
findings.reasoning: This SHA-1 invocation computes the key identifier for SubjectKeyIdentifier / AuthorityKeyIdentifier extensions, exactly as specified in RFC 5280 §4.2.1.2 (method 1: 160-bit SHA-1 hash of the value of the BIT STRING subjectPublicKey). The output is a public, standards-mandated identifier embedded in certificates and is not used for signatures, MACs, password hashing, key derivation, or any collision-sensitive security decision. Interoperability requires SHA-1 here; substituting SHA-256 would break the RFC. No secret or attacker-influenced security boundary is crossed, so this is not a weak-crypto vulnerability.

Callers: SubjectKeyIdentifier.from_public_key (line 298) and AuthorityKeyIdentifier.from_issuer_public_key (line 225).
evidence.dataflow_analysis: Input is a public key object supplied by the caller; the SHA-1 digest becomes the extension's keyIdentifier bytes in the certificate. No encryption/authentication relies on SHA-1 preimage or collision resistance here.
evidence.notes: RFC 5280-mandated key identifier derivation; occasional deprecation discussions in the project confirm it is retained for spec compliance. Also note this is an identifier over a public key, which is by definition not secret.

findings.description: CVE-2023-23931: Cipher.update_into() in the OpenSSL backend writes ciphertext into a caller-supplied buffer via ffi.from_buffer() without verifying the buffer is writable, allowing memory corruption of immutable objects (bytes).
findings.code_snippet:
def update_into(self, data: bytes, buf: bytes) -> int:
        total_data_len = len(data)
        if len(buf) < (total_data_len + self._block_size_bytes - 1):
            raise ValueError(
                "buffer must be at least {} bytes for this "
                "payload".format(len(data) + self._block_size_bytes - 1)
            )

        data_processed = 0
        total_out = 0
        outlen = self._backend._ffi.new("int *")
        baseoutbuf = self._backend._ffi.from_buffer(buf)
        baseinbuf = self._backend._ffi.from_buffer(data)

        while data_processed != total_data_len:
            outbuf = baseoutbuf + total_out
            inbuf = baseinbuf + data_processed
            inlen = min(self._MAX_CHUNK_SIZE, total_data_len - data_processed)

            res = self._backend._lib.EVP_CipherUpdate(
                self._ctx, outbuf, outlen, inbuf, inlen
            )
findings.reasoning: The only validation performed on the destination buffer `buf` is a length check (line 150). There is no check that `buf` is a mutable buffer type (bytearray/memoryview) — grep for `readonly`, `writable`, `bytearray`, `memoryview` across src/cryptography/hazmat/primitives/ciphers and the openssl backend returns no such validation. `baseoutbuf = self._backend._ffi.from_buffer(buf)` (line 159) therefore happily produces a writable C pointer even when the caller passes an immutable `bytes` object (cffi's from_buffer on bytes exposes the underlying immutable memory). That pointer is passed as the output buffer (`outbuf`) to `EVP_CipherUpdate`, so OpenSSL writes ciphertext directly over the memory backing the immutable bytes object. Because bytes objects are supposed to be immutable and may be interned/shared, this corrupts shared process memory — the exact CVE-2023-23931 (CWE-787/CWE-123 "write-what-where into immutable object") fixed in cryptography 39.0.1 by rejecting non-writable buffers. Note fixed source: same file lacks any `isinstance(buf, ...)`/writable check anywhere (file has only 281 lines; function at 148-187).
